query: Starting from a eutectic high-entropy alloy with a hierarchical microstructure of dual-phase lamellar colonies, what single intervention could overcome limited room-temperature tensile ductility and brittleness while retaining or increasing strength? The hypothesis should address the tendency for dislocation pile-ups near internal boundaries to produce local stress concentrations, microcracking, and catastrophic damage during straining. Specify the intervention, its mechanism, the predicted strength and ductility relative to the untreated starting material, the applicable testing and operating conditions, supporting prior evidence, and a falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: A targeted phase‐selective recrystallization heat treatment that preferentially recrystallizes the softer FCC lamellae while retaining the hard B2 (or BCC) lamellae and their strong semi‐coherent phase boundaries will reduce dislocation pile‐ups near internal interfaces. This treatment should alleviate localized stress concentrations and inhibit early microcracking, thereby overcoming the inherent brittleness while retaining or even boosting the overall strength.
generation.material_initial_state: Eutectic high-entropy alloy with a hierarchical dual-phase lamellar microstructure (soft FCC lamellae coexisting with hard B2/BCC lamellae featuring semi‑coherent phase boundaries)
generation.intervention: Apply a carefully controlled heat treatment (phase-selective recrystallization) at a temperature and duration that recrystallizes the soft FCC phase without coarsening or significantly altering the hard phase microstructure.
generation.conditions: Room-temperature quasi-static tensile loading; the treatment is optimized under conventional annealing conditions below the temperature that would degrade the lamellar architecture.
generation.structural_mediator: Recrystallized FCC lamellae with reduced dislocation density and eliminated precursors for dislocation pile-ups, while retaining intact strong, semi-coherent phase boundaries from the hard phase.
generation.mechanism: The soft phase, originally prone to accumulating high densities of dislocations at its interfaces, is reset by recrystallization so that during subsequent deformation it accommodates strain more homogeneously. The hard phase with its strong semi‐coherent boundaries continues to block dislocation motion effectively. This dual effect reduces local stress concentrations and delays microcrack initiation, while the preserved internal boundaries continue to promote work hardening.
generation.predicted_outcome: The recrystallized alloy is predicted to exhibit a notable increase in uniform tensile ductility (e.g., an increase from ~25% to potentially ~35% uniform elongation) while maintaining or even increasing the yield strength (e.g., in the GPa regime) compared to the as-cast or as-deformed condition.
generation.baseline: The untreated eutectic HEA typically shows limited room-temperature ductility and brittle failure due to dislocation pile-ups and microcracking at the dual-phase interfaces.
generation.boundary: This intervention is expected to be effective under quasi-static, room-temperature deformation conditions for alloys with the specified eutectic lamellar architecture; its effectiveness under high strain rates or significantly different thermal histories remains to be established.
generation.uncertainty: While literature on phase-selective recrystallization and internal boundary engineering supports this approach, the exact heat treatment parameters and the magnitude of the ductility improvement require further optimization and may vary with alloy composition and processing history.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples from the same eutectic HEA: one group undergoes the phase-selective recrystallization treatment (with parameters chosen to selectively recrystallize the FCC phase) and the other remains untreated. Conduct room-temperature quasi-static tensile tests while simultaneously monitoring the microstructural evolution (using in situ TEM or high-resolution EBSD) to quantify dislocation density distributions and crack initiation sites.
measurements: Tensile yield strength and uniform elongation
Quantitative analysis of dislocation density and pile-up at phase boundaries via microscopy
Fractography to assess microcrack initiation and propagation
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the recrystallized samples do not show a statistically significant reduction in dislocation pile-ups at internal boundaries, fail to exhibit an increase in uniform tensile ductility (e.g., an increase of at least ~20% relative to untreated samples), or if the yield strength decreases significantly compared to the untreated baseline, then the hypothesis that phase-selective recrystallization effectively overcomes the ductility limitation while retaining/increasing strength would be falsified.

Excellent ductility is crucial not only for shaping but also for strengthening metals and alloys. The ever most widely used eutectic alloys are suffering from the limited ductility and losing competitiveness among advanced structural materials. Here we report a distinctive concept of phase-selective recrystallization to overcome this challenge for eutectic alloys by triggering the strain hardening capacity of the duplex phases completely. We manipulate the strain partitioning behavior of the two phases in a eutectic high-entropy alloy (EHEA) to obtain the phase-selectively recrystallized microstructure with a fully recrystallized soft phase embedded in the skeleton of a hard phase. The resulting microstructure fully releases the strain hardening capacity in EHEA by eliminating the weak boundaries. Our phase-selectively recrystallized EHEA achieves a high ductility of ∼35% uniform elongation with true stress of ∼2 GPa. This concept is universal for various duplex alloys with soft and hard phases and opens new frontiers for traditional eutectic alloys as high-strength metallic materials.
